content.content:
1	Mounting a pull on a cabinet door or a drawer front requires two holes that satisfy three separate conditions at once. The two holes must lie at a common setback from a straight edge of the workpiece, they must be separated by the center-to-center spacing of the particular pull being installed, and the pair must sit symmetrically about a chosen centerline of the workpiece. A hole that is correct in one of these three respects and wrong in another still spoils a finished panel, and a panel that has been drilled cannot be corrected by moving the hole.
2	
3	Laying the holes out by hand with a rule and a square requires the installer to compute and mark two positions for every panel, to transfer each mark accurately, and then to start a drill bit exactly on a pencil intersection on a hard and often prefinished surface. Small errors in measuring, in marking, and in bit wander accumulate independently on each of the two holes, so the pair can be out of square with the edge even when each individual measurement was made carefully. Repeating the layout on every door and drawer front of a run multiplies both the labor and the opportunities for error.
4	
5	Simple drilling guides reduce part of this burden by presenting a hardened bushing that both positions the bit and keeps it perpendicular to the surface. A guide of that kind still leaves the installer to establish where the guide itself is placed on the panel, and a guide that fixes the two bushings at a single separation serves only one pull pattern. Adjustable arrangements in which a scale is read once and a second hole is measured from the first reintroduce the accumulation of error that the guide was meant to remove, because an error in setting the single reading displaces both holes and an error in transferring the spacing displaces only one of them.
6	
7	A further difficulty arises from the direction in which the workpiece is referenced. A pull on an upper cabinet door is commonly located from the lower edge of the door, while a pull on a drawer front or a base cabinet door is commonly located from the upper edge or from a stile edge on the opposite side. A jig whose edge fence projects from one longitudinal side of its body can be referenced from the opposite edge only by turning the whole jig over, which puts the marked and readable face of the jig against the panel where it cannot be seen, or by printing a second set of marks that runs in the opposite direction, which invites the installer to read the wrong scale. Neither expedient is satisfactory in the field, where the installer moves repeatedly between doors and drawer fronts on the same run of cabinets.
8	
9	Powered and electronically assisted layout systems can measure and record positions, but they add cost, require charging or batteries, and are unnecessary for an operation whose entire geometry is fixed by one straight edge, one centerline, and one spacing dimension.
10

1	In the following description, the terms upper, lower, above, below, inward, and downward refer to the orientation of the drilling jig when its flat lower face rests on the front face of a workpiece that is held vertically or horizontally for drilling. These terms are used for convenience of description and do not limit the orientation in which the jig may be used.
2	
3	Referring to FIG. 1, the drilling jig includes an elongated straight rail 10. The rail 10 has a flat lower face 14 (FIG. 4) that rests on the front face of a workpiece 90, and an opposite upper face 12 (FIG. 3). A straight longitudinal slot 16 runs through the rail 10 from the upper face 12 to the lower face 14 and extends along the length of the rail 10. Distance marks 18 (FIG. 2) are carried on the upper face 12 beside the longitudinal slot 16 and are printed there. The rail 10 has a first end and an opposite second end.
4	
5	The workpiece 90 is a cabinet door, a drawer front, or a like panel having a front face and at least one straight workpiece edge 92. The jig locates and guides the two holes that receive the mounting screws of a cabinet pull, and it does so in a single placement of the jig on the front face of the workpiece 90.
6	
7	A fence 30 is secured to the first end of the rail 10. The fence 30 is a fixed fence in the sense that it occupies a fixed position at the first end of the rail 10 and does not slide along the rail 10 as the guide carriages described below do. The fence 30 includes a downwardly projecting portion 32 that extends below the lower face 14 and bears against the workpiece edge 92, as shown in FIG. 4. The fence 30 is perpendicular to the rail 10, so that when the downwardly projecting portion 32 is held against the workpiece edge 92 the rail 10 extends inward across the front face of the workpiece 90 at a right angle to that edge. The fence 30 therefore fixes the setback of the jig, and of every hole guided by the jig, from the workpiece edge 92.
8	
9	Referring to FIG. 6, the fence 30 is releasably secured to the first end of the rail 10 by two screws 34 received in two corresponding mounting holes 36. The fence 30 is reversible. In a first orientation, the downwardly projecting portion 32 lies on a first longitudinal side of the rail 10. Removing the two screws 34, turning the fence 30 over, and reinstalling the two screws 34 in the same two mounting holes 36 places the fence 30 in a second orientation, in which the downwardly projecting portion 32 lies on the opposite second longitudinal side of the rail 10. In both orientations the upper face 12, and the distance marks 18 carried on it, face away from the workpiece 90 and remain visible to the user, and the distance marks 18 read in the same direction along the rail 10.
10	
11	The reversible mounting of the fence 30 addresses a practical difficulty of edge-referenced hole location. A pull on one cabinet component is commonly located from an upper edge of the component, while a pull on another component of the same run is commonly located from a lower edge. If the projecting part of an edge fence is permanently fixed to one longitudinal side of a marked rail, referencing the opposite edge requires either turning the whole tool over, which places the marked face against the panel where it cannot be read, or providing a second set of marks that runs in the opposite direction, which the user may read in error. Reversing the fence 30 alone moves the reference face to the other longitudinal side of the rail 10 while leaving the rail 10, the distance marks 18, and the carriage settings undisturbed, so that one marked face and one scale direction serve both cases and a setting already made is not lost when the reference edge changes.
12	
13	A removable spacer plate 40, shown in FIG. 4, may be fitted between the fence 30 and the workpiece edge 92. The spacer plate 40 has parallel opposite faces, one of which bears against the downwardly projecting portion 32 and the other of which bears against the workpiece edge 92. Because the two faces of the spacer plate 40 are parallel, the spacer plate 40 increases the setback of every hole guided by the jig by the thickness of the spacer plate 40 and does not change the separation between the holes or the alignment of the rail 10 with respect to the workpiece edge 92. A second setback may therefore be obtained by fitting the spacer plate 40 without disturbing a hole spacing that has already been set. The spacer plate 40 is fitted between the fence 30 and the workpiece edge 92, and it is removed by lifting it away from the fence 30.
14	
15	Referring again to FIG. 1, a first guide carriage 50 and a second guide carriage 70 are seated separately on the rail 10, one nearer to the fence 30 than the other. The two guide carriages are separate bodies. Neither guide carriage is coupled to the other, and each is positioned along the rail 10 independently of the other.
16	
17	The construction of the guide carriages is shown in FIG. 3, a cross-sectional view taken on line 3-3 of FIG. 2. The view shows the second guide carriage 70; the first guide carriage 50 is of the same construction. Each guide carriage has a body that seats on the upper face 12 of the rail 10 and a key 52 (FIG. 3) that depends from the body and passes into the longitudinal slot 16. The key 52 fits between the two long side walls of the longitudinal slot 16 and bears against them, so that the key 52 prevents the guide carriage from rotating relative to the rail 10 while allowing the guide carriage to slide along the longitudinal slot 16.

In the following description, the terms upper, lower, above, below, inward, and downward refer to the orientation of the drilling jig when its flat lower face rests on the front face of a workpiece that is held vertically or horizontally for drilling. These terms are used for convenience of description and do not limit the orientation in which the jig may be used.

Referring to FIG. 1, the drilling jig includes an elongated straight rail 10. The rail 10 has a flat lower face 14 (FIG. 4) that rests on the front face of a workpiece 90, and an opposite upper face 12 (FIG. 3). A straight longitudinal slot 16 runs through the rail 10 from the upper face 12 to the lower face 14 and extends along the length of the rail 10. Distance marks 18 (FIG. 2) are carried on the upper face 12 beside the longitudinal slot 16 and are printed there. The rail 10 has a first end and an opposite second end.

The workpiece 90 is a cabinet door, a drawer front, or a like panel having a front face and at least one straight workpiece edge 92. The jig locates and guides the two holes that receive the mounting screws of a cabinet pull, and it does so in a single placement of the jig on the front face of the workpiece 90.

A fence 30 is secured to the first end of the rail 10. The fence 30 is a fixed fence in the sense that it occupies a fixed position at the first end of the rail 10 and does not slide along the rail 10 as the guide carriages described below do. The fence 30 includes a downwardly projecting portion 32 that extends below the lower face 14 and bears against the workpiece edge 92, as shown in FIG. 4. The fence 30 is perpendicular to the rail 10, so that when the downwardly projecting portion 32 is held against the workpiece edge 92 the rail 10 extends inward across the front face of the workpiece 90 at a right angle to that edge. The fence 30 therefore fixes the setback of the jig, and of every hole guided by the jig, from the workpiece edge 92.

Referring to FIG. 6, the fence 30 is releasably secured to the first end of the rail 10 by two screws 34 received in two corresponding mounting holes 36. The fence 30 is reversible. In a first orientation, the downwardly projecting portion 32 lies on a first longitudinal side of the rail 10. Removing the two screws 34, turning the fence 30 over, and reinstalling the two screws 34 in the same two mounting holes 36 places the fence 30 in a second orientation, in which the downwardly projecting portion 32 lies on the opposite second longitudinal side of the rail 10. In both orientations the upper face 12, and the distance marks 18 carried on it, face away from the workpiece 90 and remain visible to the user, and the distance marks 18 read in the same direction along the rail 10.

The reversible mounting of the fence 30 addresses a practical difficulty of edge-referenced hole location. A pull on one cabinet component is commonly located from an upper edge of the component, while a pull on another component of the same run is commonly located from a lower edge. If the projecting part of an edge fence is permanently fixed to one longitudinal side of a marked rail, referencing the opposite edge requires either turning the whole tool over, which places the marked face against the panel where it cannot be read, or providing a second set of marks that runs in the opposite direction, which the user may read in error. Reversing the fence 30 alone moves the reference face to the other longitudinal side of the rail 10 while leaving the rail 10, the distance marks 18, and the carriage settings undisturbed, so that one marked face and one scale direction serve both cases and a setting already made is not lost when the reference edge changes.

A removable spacer plate 40, shown in FIG. 4, may be fitted between the fence 30 and the workpiece edge 92. The spacer plate 40 has parallel opposite faces, one of which bears against the downwardly projecting portion 32 and the other of which bears against the workpiece edge 92. Because the two faces of the spacer plate 40 are parallel, the spacer plate 40 increases the setback of every hole guided by the jig by the thickness of the spacer plate 40 and does not change the separation between the holes or the alignment of the rail 10 with respect to the workpiece edge 92. A second setback may therefore be obtained by fitting the spacer plate 40 without disturbing a hole spacing that has already been set. The spacer plate 40 is fitted between the fence 30 and the workpiece edge 92, and it is removed by lifting it away from the fence 30.

Referring again to FIG. 1, a first guide carriage 50 and a second guide carriage 70 are seated separately on the rail 10, one nearer to the fence 30 than the other. The two guide carriages are separate bodies. Neither guide carriage is coupled to the other, and each is positioned along the rail 10 independently of the other.

The construction of the guide carriages is shown in FIG. 3, a cross-sectional view taken on line 3-3 of FIG. 2. The view shows the second guide carriage 70; the first guide carriage 50 is of the same construction. Each guide carriage has a body that seats on the upper face 12 of the rail 10 and a key 52 (FIG. 3) that depends from the body and passes into the longitudinal slot 16. The key 52 fits between the two long side walls of the longitudinal slot 16 and bears against them, so that the key 52 prevents the guide carriage from rotating relative to the rail 10 while allowing the guide carriage to slide along the longitudinal slot 16.

Each guide carriage carries one cylindrical drill bushing 54 (FIG. 3). The drill bushing 54 has a bore that passes completely through the guide carriage and registers with the longitudinal slot 16, so that a drill bit passed down the bore of the drill bushing 54 travels through the longitudinal slot 16 and reaches the front face of the workpiece 90 beneath the rail 10. Because the key 52 holds the guide carriage against rotation and the guide carriage seats flat on the upper face 12, the bore of the drill bushing 54 of the first guide carriage 50 and the bore of the drill bushing 54 of the second guide carriage 70 are parallel to one another and perpendicular to the flat lower face 14 of the rail 10, and each hole is therefore started and driven square to the front face of the workpiece 90 at the position set on the rail 10.

The drill bushing 54 is a wear part. It is made of hardened metal and is received in the body of the guide carriage as a separate piece, so that a drill bushing 54 whose bore has been enlarged by use, or whose bore is of a diameter other than that required for the screws of a particular pull, can be withdrawn from the guide carriage and replaced.

Each guide carriage has a threaded clamp knob 58 (FIG. 1) above the rail 10. A threaded shank of the clamp knob 58 passes downward through the body of the guide carriage and through the longitudinal slot 16 and is received in a clamping shoe 60 (FIG. 3) below the rail 10. Turning the clamp knob 58 in the tightening direction draws the clamping shoe 60 upward toward the guide carriage, so that the rail 10 is clamped between the body of the guide carriage bearing on the upper face 12 and the clamping shoe 60 bearing on the lower face 14. The guide carriage is thereby locked at a chosen position along the rail 10. Turning the clamp knob 58 in the loosening direction releases the clamping shoe 60 from the lower face 14 and allows the guide carriage to slide freely along the longitudinal slot 16. The clamping shoe 60 remains below the lower face 14 and spans the longitudinal slot 16, so that it bears against the lower face 14 on each side of the longitudinal slot 16 when the clamp knob 58 is tightened and travels with the guide carriage along the rail 10 when the clamp knob 58 is loosened.

The first guide carriage 50 carries a first pointer 62 and the second guide carriage 70 carries a second pointer 82, as seen in FIG. 2. The first pointer 62 is aligned with the axis of the bore of the drill bushing 54 of the first guide carriage 50 and is readable against the distance marks 18. The second pointer 82 is aligned with the axis of the bore of the drill bushing 54 of the second guide carriage 70 and is readable against the distance marks 18. Each pointer is an index feature that stands adjacent the distance marks 18 on the upper face 12.

Because each guide carriage carries its own pointer and each pointer is read against the same distance marks 18, the position of each hole of the pair is established by its own direct reading. The difference between the reading of the first pointer 62 and the reading of the second pointer 82 is the center-to-center spacing of the two holes that the jig will guide. A misreading or a misplacement of one guide carriage displaces only the hole guided by that guide carriage and is not carried into the position of the other hole, unlike an arrangement in which one position is set from a scale and the second position is then measured from the first.

Referring to FIG. 2, the rail 10 has a transverse center index 24 at its midpoint. The transverse center index 24 is a mark that runs across the rail 10 transverse to the length of the rail 10 and marks the point midway between the ends of the rail 10. A shallow V-shaped sight notch 26 (FIG. 2) is formed in the second end of the rail 10 and is aligned with the transverse center index 24, so that a pencil centerline 94 (FIG. 2) drawn on the workpiece 90 is visible in the sight notch 26 when the jig is placed on the workpiece 90. Sighting the sight notch 26 and the transverse center index 24 together on the centerline 94 brings both of those features onto the centerline 94, and the sight notch 26 and the transverse center index 24 are spaced apart along the rail 10 so that the two sightings together fix the position of the jig on the workpiece 90 in the direction along the workpiece edge 92.

The three settings that the jig makes are separate from one another and are made against separate features. The fence 30, with or without the spacer plate 40, sets the setback of both holes from the workpiece edge 92. The readings of the first pointer 62 and the second pointer 82 against the distance marks 18 set the separation between the two holes and the position of the pair along the rail 10. The transverse center index 24 and the sight notch 26, sighted together on the centerline 94, set the position of the pair on the workpiece 90 in the direction along the workpiece edge 92. Changing one of the three settings does not disturb the other two.

In use, the user first selects the center-to-center spacing of the pull to be installed. Both clamp knobs 58 are loosened. The first guide carriage 50 and the second guide carriage 70 are slid along the longitudinal slot 16 until the reading of the first pointer 62 and the reading of the second pointer 82 against the distance marks 18 differ by the selected spacing and are centered about the transverse center index 24, that is, until the two readings lie at equal distances on opposite sides of the transverse center index 24. Both clamp knobs 58 are then tightened, locking each guide carriage to the rail 10.

The user marks a centerline 94 on the front face of the workpiece 90 and places the flat lower face 14 of the rail 10 on that front face. The downwardly projecting portion 32 of the fence 30, or the outer face of the spacer plate 40 when the spacer plate 40 is fitted, is pressed against the selected workpiece edge 92, which squares the rail 10 to that edge and fixes the setback. The jig is then slid along the workpiece edge 92 until the sight notch 26 and the transverse center index 24 are aligned with the centerline 94. Holding the jig in that position, the user drills through the drill bushing 54 of the first guide carriage 50 and through the drill bushing 54 of the second guide carriage 70. The jig is then lifted away from the workpiece 90. No part of the jig remains attached to the workpiece 90, no fastener is driven into the workpiece 90 to hold the jig, and the workpiece 90 carries only the two guided holes and the pencil centerline 94.

When the next component of the run is to be referenced from the opposite edge, the user removes the two screws 34, turns the fence 30 over, and reinstalls the two screws 34 in the two mounting holes 36. The downwardly projecting portion 32 then stands on the opposite longitudinal side of the rail 10, the upper face 12 still faces the user, and the carriage settings and the reading direction of the distance marks 18 are unchanged. The jig is used on the second component in the same way as on the first.

The rail 10, the fence 30, the bodies of the first guide carriage 50 and the second guide carriage 70, the clamping shoes 60, the spacer plate 40, the first pointer 62, the second pointer 82, and the clamp knobs 58 may be made of rigid polymer or of metal. The drill bushings 54 are made of hardened metal. The distance marks 18, the transverse center index 24, and the pointers may be printed features.

The jig is a hand tool and is operated entirely by hand. The jig has no motor, no battery, no electronic sensor, and no network connection, and it requires no power source of any kind. Every setting is made mechanically and is read directly from the distance marks 18, the transverse center index 24, and the sight notch 26.

The foregoing description of embodiments is illustrative. The rail 10 may be of any length sufficient to span the pull patterns to be drilled, the distance marks 18 may be graduated in any convenient unit, and the drill bushings 54 may be provided in a set of bore diameters. The features described above may be used in combinations other than those expressly described, and the scope of protection sought is defined by the claims that follow.

Most of the draft traces cleanly: the rail, upper/lower faces, longitudinal slot, printed distance marks, fixed fence at the first end with a downwardly projecting portion perpendicular to the rail, the two-screw reversible mounting, the spacer plate with parallel faces and its setback-only effect, two separate carriages with anti-rotation keys, cylindrical hardened-metal replaceable bushings whose bores register with the slot and are parallel and perpendicular to the lower face, clamp knob / threaded shank / clamping shoe, the two independent pointers and the difference-equals-spacing result, the transverse center index at the midpoint, the shallow V sight notch in the second end aligned with the index, the full method of use, the lift-away/no-attachment result, the polymer-or-metal material list, and the no-motor/battery/sensor/network limitation all map to exact disclosure sentences.

Seventeen items do not. The critical untraced additions are: (1) the clamping shoe "spans the longitudinal slot" and bears on the lower face "on each side" of it (claim 12 and ¶23) — the source says only that the shoe is below the rail and that the rail is clamped between carriage and shoe; (2) the key "bearing against side walls of the longitudinal slot" (claim 1) and "fits between the two long side walls ... and bears against them" (¶17) — a contact-topology statement absent from the source; (3) bushings of differing bore diameter (claim 23, ¶21, ¶43) — the source discloses only replaceable hardened-metal wear parts; (4) FIG. 7's assertion that the pencil centerline runs "lengthwise in the same direction as the rail", lies on the band's lengthwise centre, is seen through the slot, and "passes the point where the transverse center index 24 meets the longitudinal slot 16" — the source says only that the user aligns the index and the notch with a pencil centerline and never fixes the centerline's direction relative to the rail; and (5) the ¶43 variant clauses ("any length sufficient to span the pull patterns", marks "graduated in any convenient unit").

Substantive functional-surface geometry that must come out under the v10 rule: claim 6's "the sight notch opens through an end edge of the second end of the rail, such that a centerline ... is visible in the sight notch" (runout direction and visibility for a functional notch), the matching ¶29 clause, and FIG. 7's "opening outward away from the rail 10 and centered on the lengthwise center of the band" plus "The workpiece 90 is seen in the opening of the sight notch 26."

A real internal-logic conflict: ¶7, claim 13 and claim 18 add "at a right angle to that edge / to the straight edge," which the disclosure never says. That reading cannot coexist with the draft's own reversible-fence teaching (a projecting portion that lies on a longitudinal *side* of the rail bears on an edge running alongside the rail) or with the Background premise that "The two holes must lie at a common setback from a straight edge." The source wording ("the rail extends inward across the workpiece") should be restored verbatim.

Figure and numeral defects: reference numerals 52 (key), 54 (drill bushing), 58 (clamp knob) and 60 (clamping shoe) are each used for two different physical parts — FIG. 3 applies 54 and 58 to the second carriage 70 while FIG. 5 applies the same numerals to the first carriage 50 — so a numbered part does not mean one thing. ¶29 says "Referring to FIG. 2" and cites 24, 26 and 94 to FIG. 2, but FIG. 2's brief shows none of those three; FIG. 5 and FIG. 7 are never referenced anywhere in the detailed description; the Brief Description calls FIG. 5 "a guide carriage" while the brief and numerals show the first guide carriage 50. ¶7 cites FIG. 4 for the projecting portion bearing against the workpiece edge, but FIG. 4 is the view with the spacer plate 40 interposed between them. The Brief Description of the Drawings and FIGS. 1–5 call the tool a "drill guide" while the claims, abstract and description call it a "drilling jig"; FIG. 3 uses "bore" for the carriage's receiving bore while the claims use "bore" for the bushing's own bore.

Minor untraced matter: ¶39's statement that the transverse center index and the pointers "may be printed features" (the source prints only the distance marks and makes the pointers of polymer or metal — the same paragraph says both); ¶1's "held vertically or horizontally for drilling"; claim 24 / ¶35's negative limitation "no fastener is driven into the workpiece" and ¶41's "requires no power source of any kind"; and small verbalized figure geometry (slot "rounded ends" and centring in FIG. 2, bushing "in the center of the carriage" in FIG. 5, pointer "projecting from the side of that carriage", and un-labelled generic rectangular carriage bodies).

No drafting notes, placeholders, open questions or unresolved alternatives remain in any file. Section line 3-3 is designated consistently in FIG. 2's brief, FIG. 3's brief, and the drawing description. Every fix below is a deletion or a conforming amendment that leaves the application filing-clean; where a claim is cancelled, renumber the remaining claims consecutively and update all dependencies.

findings.title: Clamping shoe "spans the longitudinal slot" and bears on each side of it is untraced
findings.detail: Claim 12 and the closing sentence of ¶23 add a structural and contact-topology relationship between the clamping shoe and the slot that no inventor passage states. The disclosure describes only that the shank passes through the slot into a shoe below the rail and that the rail is clamped between carriage and shoe. There is no affirmative passage stating that the shoe spans the slot, that it bears on each side of the slot, or that it travels with the carriage when loosened.
findings.evidence: Candidate (¶23): "The clamping shoe 60 remains below the lower face 14 and spans the longitudinal slot 16, so that it bears against the lower face 14 on each side of the longitudinal slot 16 when the clamp knob 58 is tightened and travels with the guide carriage along the rail 10 when the clamp knob 58 is loosened." Candidate (claim 12): "wherein the clamping shoe of each guide carriage remains below the lower face of the rail and spans the longitudinal slot, so as to bear against the lower face of the rail...". Nearest source (disclosure.md ¶ on carriages): "A threaded shank of the knob passes through the carriage and the longitudinal slot into a clamping shoe below the rail. Turning the knob draws the shoe toward the carriage and clamps the rail between the carriage and the shoe." No source passage mentions the shoe spanning the slot or bearing on each side of it.
findings.fix: In ¶23 replace the final sentence with: "The clamping shoe 60 remains below the lower face 14 and bears against the lower face 14 when the clamp knob 58 is tightened." Amend claim 12 to read: "12. The drilling jig of claim 1, wherein the clamping shoe of each guide carriage is disposed below the lower face of the rail and bears against the lower face of the rail when the clamp knob of that guide carriage is tightened and is released from the lower face of the rail when that clamp knob is loosened."

findings.title: Key "bearing against side walls of the longitudinal slot" is untraced contact topology
findings.detail: Claim 1 recites the key as bearing against the slot side walls, and ¶17 adds that the key fits between the two long side walls and bears against them. The disclosure states only the function of the key (anti-rotation while sliding) and never describes any bearing contact with, or fit between, the slot walls.
findings.evidence: Candidate (claim 1): "a key depending into the longitudinal slot and bearing against side walls of the longitudinal slot so as to prevent rotation of that guide carriage relative to the rail". Candidate (¶17): "The key 52 fits between the two long side walls of the longitudinal slot 16 and bears against them, so that the key 52 prevents the guide carriage from rotating relative to the rail 10...". Nearest source: "Each carriage has a lower key that passes into the longitudinal slot, and the key prevents the carriage from rotating while allowing it to slide along the slot." The disclosure contains no statement about slot side walls or bearing contact.
findings.fix: Amend claim 1 to: "a key depending into the longitudinal slot so as to prevent rotation of that guide carriage relative to the rail while permitting that guide carriage to slide along the longitudinal slot,". In ¶17 replace the sentence with: "The key 52 prevents the guide carriage from rotating relative to the rail 10 while allowing the guide carriage to slide along the longitudinal slot 16."

findings.title: Drill bushings of different bore diameters are untraced
findings.detail: The draft adds interchangeable bushings of differing bore diameter, and a set of bore diameters, as an embodiment and as a method claim. The disclosure discloses only that the bushings are replaceable wear parts of hardened metal; it never mentions bore diameter, diameter selection, or a set of sizes.
findings.evidence: Candidate (claim 23): "further comprising withdrawing the drill bushing ... and installing in that guide carriage another drill bushing having a bore of a different diameter." Candidate (¶21): "or whose bore is of a diameter other than that required for the screws of a particular pull". Candidate (¶43): "and the drill bushings 54 may be provided in a set of bore diameters." Nearest source: "The drill bushings are replaceable wear parts and are made from hardened metal." No source passage refers to bore diameter or to a set of bushings.
findings.fix: Cancel claim 23 (renumber claim 24 to 23). In ¶21 delete ", or whose bore is of a diameter other than that required for the screws of a particular pull," so the sentence reads "...so that a drill bushing 54 whose bore has been enlarged by use can be withdrawn from the guide carriage and replaced." In ¶43 delete ", and the drill bushings 54 may be provided in a set of bore diameters".

findings.title: FIG. 7 fixes the centerline's orientation and path relative to the rail, which no source passage states
findings.detail: The figure brief verbalizes a substantive geometric relationship between the workpiece centerline and the jig: that the centerline runs lengthwise in the rail's direction, lies on the band's lengthwise centre, is seen through the longitudinal slot, and passes the point where the transverse center index meets the slot. The disclosure says only that the user aligns the center index and the sight notch with a pencil centerline; it never states the centerline's direction relative to the rail, never says the centerline is seen through the slot, and never describes the index meeting the slot. These are relative-location and topology statements, not a generic outline convention, and the brief does not label them schematic.
findings.evidence: Candidate: "A centerline 94 is a single straight line drawn on the workpiece 90, running lengthwise in the same direction as the rail 10 and lying on the lengthwise center of the band. The centerline 94 appears on the workpiece 90 beyond the second end of the rail 10, within the opening of the sight notch 26, and within the longitudinal slot 16 where the workpiece 90 is seen through that opening. The centerline 94 passes the point where the transverse center index 24 meets the longitudinal slot 16." Also: "A transverse center index 24 is a short straight mark on the upper surface of the rail 10 at the left part of the fragment, running across the band transverse to the length of the rail 10 and meeting the longitudinal slot 16." Nearest source: "The rail has a transverse center index at its midpoint. A shallow V-shaped sight notch is formed in the second end of the rail and aligned with the center index. The user can align the center index and the sight notch with a pencil centerline on the workpiece."
findings.fix: Replace the two quoted paragraphs of figures/FIG-7.md with: "A transverse center index 24 is a short straight mark on the upper surface of the rail 10, running across the band transverse to the length of the rail 10 at the midpoint of the rail 10." and "A centerline 94 is a single straight line drawn on the workpiece 90 and is aligned with the transverse center index 24 and with the sight notch 26." Delete the clauses stating that the centerline runs lengthwise in the same direction as the rail, that it lies on the lengthwise center of the band, that it is seen within the longitudinal slot 16, and that the index meets the longitudinal slot.

findings.title: Untraced embodiment variants in the closing paragraph
findings.detail: The closing paragraph adds two optional variants that no inventor passage supports: an unrestricted rail length keyed to spanning "the pull patterns to be drilled", and distance marks "graduated in any convenient unit". The disclosure says nothing about rail length or about units of graduation.
findings.evidence: Candidate: "The rail 10 may be of any length sufficient to span the pull patterns to be drilled, the distance marks 18 may be graduated in any convenient unit, and the drill bushings 54 may be provided in a set of bore diameters." Nearest source: "The tool has an elongated straight rail... Distance marks are printed along the upper face beside the slot." There is no affirmative statement about length or units.
findings.fix: Replace ¶43 with: "The foregoing description of embodiments is illustrative. The features described above may be used in combinations other than those expressly described, and the scope of protection sought is defined by the claims that follow."

findings.title: Claim 21 introduces a second workpiece and an opposite-side reference edge that the disclosure does not describe
findings.detail: Claim 21 recites drilling a second, distinct workpiece whose reference edge is on the opposite side of that second workpiece from the edge used on the first workpiece, and requires that the carriage positions be unaltered across the fence reversal. The disclosure's reversal teaching is confined to letting the same marked upper face serve when the tool is referenced from an upper or a lower edge; it never describes a second workpiece, an opposite-side edge relation between two workpieces, or a preserved setting across a reversal.
findings.evidence: Candidate: "further comprising, after reinstalling the two screws and without altering the positions of the first guide carriage and the second guide carriage along the rail, placing the flat lower face on a front face of a second workpiece, pressing the downwardly projecting portion against a straight edge of the second workpiece that is on an opposite side of the second workpiece from the straight edge of the workpiece...". Nearest source: "This lets the same marked upper face be used when the tool is referenced from either an upper edge or a lower edge of a workpiece." No source passage mentions a second workpiece or an unaltered carriage setting.
findings.fix: Cancel claim 21 and renumber claims 22–24 consecutively (updating their dependencies on claim 18). Correspondingly, in ¶11 delete ", so that one marked face and one scale direction serve both cases and a setting already made is not lost when the reference edge changes" and end the sentence after "...leaving the rail 10, the distance marks 18, and the carriage settings undisturbed."

findings.title: Sight-notch runout direction and centerline visibility are untraced functional-surface geometry
findings.where: draft/09-claims.md claim 6; draft/08-detailed-description.md ¶29; figures/FIG-7.md (sight notch paragraph)
findings.detail: Claim 6, ¶29 and FIG. 7 state where the notch runs out (through the end edge, opening outward away from the rail), where it sits circumferentially on the end (centred on the lengthwise centre), and that the workpiece and the centerline are visible in its opening. For a functional sight notch these runout-direction, end-position and visibility statements are substantive even under a schematic label, and the disclosure supplies none of them.
findings.evidence: Candidate (claim 6): "wherein the sight notch opens through an end edge of the second end of the rail, such that a centerline marked on the front face of the workpiece is visible in the sight notch when the flat lower face rests on the front face...". Candidate (¶29): "...so that a pencil centerline 94 (FIG. 2) drawn on the workpiece 90 is visible in the sight notch 26 when the jig is placed on the workpiece 90." Candidate (FIG-7): "A sight notch 26 is a shallow V-shaped notch cut into the end edge at the second end of the rail 10, opening outward away from the rail 10 and centered on the lengthwise center of the band. The workpiece 90 is seen in the opening of the sight notch 26." Nearest source: "A shallow V-shaped sight notch is formed in the second end of the rail and aligned with the center index."
findings.fix: Amend claim 6 to: "6. The drilling jig of claim 5, wherein the sight notch and the transverse center index are spaced apart along the rail and are alignable together with a centerline marked on the front face of the workpiece." In ¶29 replace "so that a pencil centerline 94 (FIG. 2) drawn on the workpiece 90 is visible in the sight notch 26 when the jig is placed on the workpiece 90" with "for alignment with a pencil centerline 94 (FIG. 7) drawn on the workpiece 90". In figures/FIG-7.md replace the notch paragraph with: "A sight notch 26 is a shallow V-shaped notch formed in the second end of the rail 10 and aligned with the transverse center index 24."

findings.title: Added "at a right angle to the straight edge" conflicts with the reversible-fence structure and the Background premise
findings.detail: The disclosure states that the fence is perpendicular to the rail and that the rail "extends inward across the workpiece"; it never states the angle between the rail and the referenced edge. The draft adds that the rail extends "at a right angle to that edge". That added relationship cannot coexist with the draft's own reversible-fence structure, in which the downwardly projecting portion lies on a longitudinal side of the rail and is moved to the opposite longitudinal side so that the tool can be referenced from an upper or a lower edge — a portion lying alongside a longitudinal side bears on an edge running alongside the rail, not at a right angle to it. It also contradicts the Background premise that both holes lie at a common setback, since two bushings spaced along a rail set at a right angle to the edge cannot be equidistant from it.
findings.evidence: Candidate (¶7): "...the rail 10 extends inward across the front face of the workpiece 90 at a right angle to that edge." Candidate (claims 13 and 18): "so that the rail extends inward across the front face at a right angle to the straight edge". Conflicting draft text (¶9): "the downwardly projecting portion 32 lies on a first longitudinal side of the rail 10 ... places the fence 30 in a second orientation, in which the downwardly projecting portion 32 lies on the opposite second longitudinal side of the rail 10." Conflicting draft text (05-background ¶1): "The two holes must lie at a common setback from a straight edge of the workpiece." Source: "The fence is perpendicular to the rail, so the rail extends inward across the workpiece when the fence bears against the edge."
findings.fix: Delete "at a right angle to that edge" in ¶7 so the clause ends "...the rail 10 extends inward across the front face of the workpiece 90." Delete "at a right angle to the straight edge" from claim 13 and from claim 18 so each reads "so that the rail extends inward across the front face."

findings.title: Reference numerals 52, 54, 58 and 60 each designate two different parts
findings.detail: The key, drill bushing, clamp knob and clamping shoe of both carriages carry a single numeral each, so one numbered part does not mean one thing. FIG. 3 applies 54 and 58 to the parts of the second guide carriage 70, while FIG. 5 applies the same numerals 54 and 58 to the parts of the first guide carriage 50, and the description uses 54 for both bushings in one sentence. The numeral scheme already distinguishes the carriages (50/70) and the pointers (62/82), so the shared numerals are an inconsistency rather than a convention.
findings.evidence: Candidate (¶19): "the bore of the drill bushing 54 of the first guide carriage 50 and the bore of the drill bushing 54 of the second guide carriage 70 are parallel to one another". FIG-3 numeral list: "52: key, 54: drill bushing, 58: clamp knob, 60: clamping shoe, 70: second guide carriage." FIG-5 numeral list: "50: first guide carriage, 54: drill bushing, 58: clamp knob, 62: first pointer." ¶39: "the clamping shoes 60 ... and the clamp knobs 58" (plural parts, single numerals).
findings.fix: Assign the second guide carriage's parts distinct numerals: key 72, drill bushing 74, clamp knob 78, clamping shoe 80. Add these four rows to draft/numerals.md; change FIG-3.md's text and numeral list to 72, 74, 78, 80; in ¶19 write "the bore of the drill bushing 54 of the first guide carriage 50 and the bore of the drill bushing 74 of the second guide carriage 70"; in ¶23 and ¶33 refer to "the clamp knob 58 and the clamp knob 78" and "the clamping shoe 60 and the clamping shoe 80"; in ¶17 write "a key 52 of the first guide carriage 50 and a like key 72 of the second guide carriage 70"; in ¶35 and ¶39 list both numerals of each pair.

findings.title: Description cites FIG. 2 for elements FIG. 2 does not show, and never references FIG. 5 or FIG. 7
findings.where: draft/08-detailed-description.md ¶29; draft/07-drawings.md FIG. 5; figures/FIG-2.md; figures/FIG-5.md; figures/FIG-7.md
findings.detail: ¶29 opens "Referring to FIG. 2" and cites the transverse center index 24, sight notch 26 and centerline 94 to FIG. 2, but FIG. 2's brief depicts none of those three numerals. The elements are depicted only in FIG. 7, which the detailed description never cites. FIG. 5 is likewise never cited anywhere in the description, and the Brief Description calls it "a guide carriage" while the figure brief and its numeral list show the first guide carriage 50.
findings.evidence: Candidate (¶29): "Referring to FIG. 2, the rail 10 has a transverse center index 24 at its midpoint. ... A shallow V-shaped sight notch 26 (FIG. 2) is formed in the second end of the rail 10 ... so that a pencil centerline 94 (FIG. 2) drawn on the workpiece 90...". FIG-2 numeral list: "10, 16, 18, 30, 50, 62, 70, 82" — 24, 26 and 94 do not appear. FIG-7 numeral list: "10, 16, 24, 26, 90, 94." Brief Description: "FIG. 5 is a detail top plan view of a guide carriage of the drill guide of FIG. 2." FIG-5 brief: "A detail top plan view of the first guide carriage of FIG. 2."
findings.fix: In ¶29 change "Referring to FIG. 2" to "Referring to FIG. 7" and change both parentheticals "(FIG. 2)" to "(FIG. 7)". In ¶25, after the first sentence, add "The first guide carriage 50 is shown in detail in FIG. 5." In draft/07-drawings.md change the FIG. 5 entry to "FIG. 5 is a detail top plan view of the first guide carriage of the drilling jig of FIG. 2."

findings.title: ¶7 cites FIG. 4 for the fence bearing directly on the workpiece edge, but FIG. 4 interposes the spacer plate
findings.detail: ¶7 says the downwardly projecting portion bears against the workpiece edge "as shown in FIG. 4", but FIG. 4 is expressly the view with the spacer plate 40 fitted between the projecting portion 32 and the workpiece edge 92, so in that figure the portion bears on the spacer plate, not on the edge.
findings.evidence: Candidate (¶7): "The fence 30 includes a downwardly projecting portion 32 that extends below the lower face 14 and bears against the workpiece edge 92, as shown in FIG. 4." FIG-4 brief: "The spacer plate 40 is between the downwardly projecting portion 32 of the fence and the workpiece edge 92." Brief Description: "FIG. 4 is a side elevation view of the drill guide on a workpiece with a spacer plate installed."
findings.fix: In ¶7 replace ", as shown in FIG. 4" with " (see FIG. 1)" so the sentence reads "...extends below the lower face 14 and bears against the workpiece edge 92 (see FIG. 1)."

findings.title: "drill guide" in the Brief Description and figure briefs versus "drilling jig" everywhere else
findings.where: draft/07-drawings.md FIGS. 1–5; figures/FIG-1.md, FIG-2.md, FIG-3.md, FIG-4.md, FIG-5.md; draft/08-detailed-description.md; draft/09-claims.md
findings.detail: The claims, abstract, summary and detailed description consistently call the article a "drilling jig" (or "the jig"), while the Brief Description of the Drawings and five figure briefs call it a "drill guide". The same apparatus must carry one designation across the text and the drawings.
findings.evidence: Candidate (07-drawings.md): "FIG. 1 is a perspective view of a drill guide on a workpiece." / "FIG. 2 is a top plan view of the drill guide of FIG. 1." Candidate (FIG-1.md): "A perspective view of a drill guide assembly on a workpiece 90." Compare (¶3): "Referring to FIG. 1, the drilling jig includes an elongated straight rail 10." Compare (claim 1): "A drilling jig for locating and guiding a pair of holes...".
findings.fix: In draft/07-drawings.md and in the opening line of figures/FIG-1.md through FIG-5.md, replace every occurrence of "drill guide" and "drill guide assembly" with "drilling jig".

findings.title: Center index and pointers stated to be printed features, which the source does not disclose and the same paragraph contradicts
findings.detail: The disclosure states that only the distance marks are printed, and it lists the pointers among the parts that may be made of rigid polymer or metal. Saying the center index and the pointers "may be printed features" is untraced and sits inconsistently beside the immediately preceding sentence of the same paragraph, which makes the pointers of polymer or metal.
findings.evidence: Candidate (¶39): "The distance marks 18, the transverse center index 24, and the pointers may be printed features." Preceding sentence of the same paragraph: "...the first pointer 62, the second pointer 82, and the clamp knobs 58 may be made of rigid polymer or of metal." Source: "Distance marks are printed along the upper face beside the slot." and "The rail, fence, carriage bodies, shoes, spacer plate, pointers, and knobs may be made from rigid polymer or metal."
findings.fix: Delete the final sentence of ¶39. (¶3 already states that the distance marks 18 are printed on the upper face 12.)

findings.title: Untraced negative limitations about fasteners and power sources
findings.detail: The draft adds two negative statements beyond the source: that no fastener is driven into the workpiece to hold the jig, and that the jig "requires no power source of any kind". The disclosure supports only that no part remains attached to the workpiece and that the tool has no motor, battery, electronic sensor, or network connection.
findings.evidence: Candidate (claim 24): "wherein the drilling jig is held against the workpiece by hand during the drilling, no fastener is driven into the workpiece to hold the drilling jig...". Candidate (¶35): "no fastener is driven into the workpiece 90 to hold the jig". Candidate (¶41): "and it requires no power source of any kind". Source: "The tool is then lifted away. No part remains attached to the workpiece." and "The tool has no motor, battery, electronic sensor, or network connection."
findings.fix: Amend claim 24 to: "wherein the drilling jig is held against the workpiece by hand during the drilling, no part of the drilling jig remains attached to the workpiece, and the drilling jig is operated without a motor, a battery, an electronic sensor, or a network connection." In ¶35 delete ", no fastener is driven into the workpiece 90 to hold the jig,". In ¶41 delete ", and it requires no power source of any kind".

findings.title: Untraced operating condition in the orientation-terms paragraph
findings.detail: The orientation convention adds an operating condition — that the workpiece is held vertically or horizontally for drilling — that no inventor passage states. The disclosure describes the lower face resting on the front face of a cabinet door or drawer front without specifying how the workpiece is held.
findings.evidence: Candidate: "...refer to the orientation of the drilling jig when its flat lower face rests on the front face of a workpiece that is held vertically or horizontally for drilling." Nearest source: "The tool has an elongated straight rail with a flat lower face that rests on the front face of a cabinet door or drawer front."
findings.fix: In ¶1 delete "that is held vertically or horizontally for drilling" so the clause reads "...when its flat lower face rests on the front face of a workpiece."

findings.title: "bore" designates two different features in FIG. 3 and in the claims
findings.detail: The claims and description use "bore" for the bushing's own through-bore, while the FIG. 3 brief uses "bore" for the carriage opening that receives the bushing. One term should not carry two meanings across the text and the drawings.
findings.evidence: Candidate (FIG-3): "A drill bushing 54 is seated in a vertical bore through the carriage 70, aligned with the slot 16." Compare (claim 1): "a cylindrical drill bushing having a bore that passes completely through that guide carriage and registers with the longitudinal slot". Source: "Each carriage carries one cylindrical drill bushing with a vertical bore. The bore passes completely through the carriage...".
findings.fix: In figures/FIG-3.md replace the sentence with: "A cylindrical drill bushing 54 is carried by the carriage 70, its vertical bore passing completely through the carriage 70 and aligned with the slot 16."

findings.title: Untraced geometric particulars in the plan-view figure briefs, and unlabelled generic carriage outlines
findings.detail: The plan-view briefs verbalize relative locations and shape particulars that the disclosure does not state: the slot centred lengthwise on the rail with rounded ends stopping short of both rail ends, the pointer projecting from the side of the carriage, and the bushing located in the centre of the carriage. The disclosure states only that the slot is straight and longitudinal and runs through the rail, that the pointer is aligned with the bushing axis and readable against the marks, and that the bore passes completely through the carriage. In addition, the carriage bodies are given a rectangular outline without the schematic label that the fence in the same brief carries.
findings.evidence: Candidate (FIG-2): "A longitudinal slot 16 runs lengthwise along the center of the rail 10 as an elongated opening with rounded ends, both ends of the slot 16 stopping short of the ends of the rail 10." / "The first guide carriage 50 and the second guide carriage 70 are two separate rectangular bodies resting on top of the rail 10" / "A first pointer 62 is a short index line on the first guide carriage 50, projecting from the side of that carriage toward the distance marks 18". Candidate (FIG-5): "The drill bushing 54 is in the center of the carriage 50." Nearest source: "A straight longitudinal slot runs through the rail." / "The bore passes completely through the carriage and aligns with an opening through the slot..." / "The first carriage has a pointer aligned with its bushing axis and readable against the distance marks."
findings.fix: In figures/FIG-2.md replace the slot sentence with "A longitudinal slot 16 runs lengthwise along the rail 10 as a straight elongated opening, shown schematically."; replace "are two separate rectangular bodies resting on top of the rail 10" with "are two separate bodies, shown schematically as plain rectangular bodies, resting on top of the rail 10"; and replace "projecting from the side of that carriage toward the distance marks 18 and ending beside them" with "aligned with the axis of the bore of that carriage and ending beside the distance marks 18" (and likewise for the second pointer 82). In figures/FIG-5.md replace "The drill bushing 54 is in the center of the carriage 50." with "The drill bushing 54 is carried by the carriage 50, its bore passing through the carriage 50."

The critical untraced additions are: (1) the clamping shoe "spans the longitudinal slot" and bears on the lower face "on each side" of it (claim 12 and ¶23) — the source says only that the shoe is below the rail and that the rail is clamped between carriage and shoe; (2) the key "bearing against side walls of the longitudinal slot" (claim 1) and "fits between the two long side walls ... and bears against them" (¶17) — a contact-topology statement absent from the source; (3) bushings of differing bore diameter (claim 23, ¶21, ¶43) — the source discloses only replaceable hardened-metal wear parts; (4) FIG. 7's assertion that the pencil centerline runs "lengthwise in the same direction as the rail", lies on the band's lengthwise centre, is seen through the slot, and "passes the point where the transverse center index 24 meets the longitudinal slot 16" — the source says only that the user aligns the index and the notch with a pencil centerline and never fixes the centerline's direction relative to the rail; and (5) the ¶43 variant clauses ("any length sufficient to span the pull patterns", marks "graduated in any convenient unit").

Substantive functional-surface geometry that must come out under the v10 rule: claim 6's "the sight notch opens through an end edge of the second end of the rail, such that a centerline ... is visible in the sight notch" (runout direction and visibility for a functional notch), the matching ¶29 clause, and FIG. 7's "opening outward away from the rail 10 and centered on the lengthwise center of the band" plus "The workpiece 90 is seen in the opening of the sight notch 26."

A real internal-logic conflict: ¶7, claim 13 and claim 18 add "at a right angle to that edge / to the straight edge," which the disclosure never says. That reading cannot coexist with the draft's own reversible-fence teaching (a projecting portion that lies on a longitudinal *side* of the rail bears on an edge running alongside the rail) or with the Background premise that "The two holes must lie at a common setback from a straight edge." The source wording ("the rail extends inward across the workpiece") should be restored verbatim.

Figure and numeral defects: reference numerals 52 (key), 54 (drill bushing), 58 (clamp knob) and 60 (clamping shoe) are each used for two different physical parts — FIG. 3 applies 54 and 58 to the second carriage 70 while FIG. 5 applies the same numerals to the first carriage 50 — so a numbered part does not mean one thing. ¶29 says "Referring to FIG. 2" and cites 24, 26 and 94 to FIG. 2, but FIG. 2's brief shows none of those three; FIG. 5 and FIG. 7 are never referenced anywhere in the detailed description; the Brief Description calls FIG. 5 "a guide carriage" while the brief and numerals show the first guide carriage 50. ¶7 cites FIG. 4 for the projecting portion bearing against the workpiece edge, but FIG. 4 is the view with the spacer plate 40 interposed between them. The Brief Description of the Drawings and FIGS. 1–5 call the tool a "drill guide" while the claims, abstract and description call it a "drilling jig"; FIG. 3 uses "bore" for the carriage's receiving bore while the claims use "bore" for the bushing's own bore.

Minor untraced matter: ¶39's statement that the transverse center index and the pointers "may be printed features" (the source prints only the distance marks and makes the pointers of polymer or metal — the same paragraph says both); ¶1's "held vertically or horizontally for drilling"; claim 24 / ¶35's negative limitation "no fastener is driven into the workpiece" and ¶41's "requires no power source of any kind"; and small verbalized figure geometry (slot "rounded ends" and centring in FIG. 2, bushing "in the center of the carriage" in FIG. 5, pointer "projecting from the side of that carriage", and un-labelled generic rectangular carriage bodies).

No drafting notes, placeholders, open questions or unresolved alternatives remain in any file. Section line 3-3 is designated consistently in FIG. 2's brief, FIG. 3's brief, and the drawing description. Every fix below is a deletion or a conforming amendment that leaves the application filing-clean; where a claim is cancelled, renumber the remaining claims consecutively and update all dependencies.

findings.title: Added "at a right angle to the straight edge" conflicts with the reversible-fence structure and the Background premise
